title: Composition, context, forms, performance
blurb: Context, compound components, forms, optimistic updates, accessibility and routing — the parts of React you get asked about once past the basics.

questions.q: What does Context cost you, compared with passing props?
choices: Nothing: it replaces a state library with no downsides at any scale
Its values are global, so they persist across full page reloads
Every consumer re-renders whenever the provided value changes
It memoises the subtree below, so children can show stale values
questions.why: Context is dependency injection, not a state manager. If a fast-changing value shares a provider with a slow-changing one, every consumer re-renders; split the contexts or memoise the value. It holds nothing across reloads.
questions.asked: 'When would you use context?' The weak answer is 'instead of Redux, for all state'.

questions.q: Why does this provider re-render every consumer on each parent render?
questions.code: <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
choices: The object literal is a new reference on every render
Providers always re-render every consumer, whatever the value
`setTheme` from `useState` changes identity every render
Context compares values deeply, which forces the re-render
questions.why: Context compares the value with `Object.is`, and `{{ ... }}` is a new object each time. Wrap it: `useMemo(() => ({ theme, setTheme }), [theme])`. `setTheme` is already stable, so it is not the cause.
questions.asked: It tests whether you can spot the reference-equality cost of context in code review.

questions.q: What is prop drilling?
choices: Passing so many props to one component that its signature is unreadable
Mutating a prop inside a child so the parent sees the changed value
Forwarding every prop to a child with the spread syntax `{...props}`
Passing props through components that do not use them, to reach a child
questions.why: It is usually fine at two or three levels: explicit and greppable. Reaching for context at the first sign of it replaces a visible data flow with an invisible one, and composition (passing elements as children) often removes the drilling with no context at all.
questions.asked: The follow-up, 'is it always bad?', is where the composition answer earns credit.

questions.q: `count` lives in the parent. Why can `Slow` re-render without re-rendering `Fast`?
questions.code: <Slow><Fast count={count} /></Slow>
choices: React memoises `children` automatically for every component
`children` was created by the parent, so the element is unchanged
It cannot: `children` always re-renders along with its parent
Only because `Slow` is a class component with its own lifecycle
questions.why: The `<Fast>` element object was made in the parent's render. If `Slow` re-renders for its own reasons, React sees the identical element and skips that subtree. It is memoisation without `memo`, and React does not memoise `children` in general.
questions.asked: A sophisticated answer to 'how would you optimise this tree?'.

questions.q: What are compound components?
choices: Components that render other components inside their own JSX
Components that share implicit state through context, like Tabs and Tab
Functions that take a component and return an enhanced component
Components whose logic is assembled from several different custom hooks
questions.why: `<Tabs><Tab /></Tabs>` lets the consumer compose markup naturally instead of passing a config array. The cost is a less explicit API and a required parent, so the pattern earns its place mainly in design systems. A function that returns an enhanced component is a higher-order component, a different pattern.
questions.asked: It comes up when designing reusable UI, and shows familiarity with how component libraries are built.

questions.q: What is an optimistic update?
choices: Retrying a failed request automatically until the server accepts it
Prefetching data the user is likely to need before they ask for it
Skipping error handling on the assumption the server stays healthy
Showing the change in the UI at once and rolling back if it fails
questions.why: It makes an app feel instant. It needs the previous state kept for rollback and a visible message when the rollback happens; silently reverting is worse than a spinner.
questions.asked: Common for frontend roles; the follow-up is 'how do you handle the failure case?'.

questions.q: Which validation timing avoids flagging a field while the user is still typing, yet clears the error as soon as it is fixed?
choices: Validate on blur, then on change once the field has shown an error
Validate on every keystroke from the moment the field is focused
Validate only on submit, and keep errors until the next submit
Validate only on the server and show its errors after a round trip
questions.why: Keystroke validation shows 'invalid email' after the second character. Validating on blur waits until the user leaves the field; switching that field to live validation once it has errored lets the message clear as they fix it. The server must validate regardless.
questions.asked: It tests form UX judgement, which separates developers who have watched users fill in forms.

questions.q: Your React form's Submit can be clicked twice before the first request returns. What is the client-side fix?
choices: Debounce the submit handler by 300 ms so rapid clicks collapse
Wrap the submit handler in `useCallback` so it is created once
Track an in-flight flag in state and disable the button while set
Call `event.preventDefault()` at the top of the submit handler
questions.why: A `submitting` flag set before the request and cleared after it blocks the second click for exactly as long as needed. A debounce only delays, `useCallback` changes identity not behaviour, and `preventDefault` stops navigation, not a second call. The server still needs idempotency for retries; that is a separate, server-side fix.
questions.asked: Double submits create duplicate orders; interviewers want the client fix and awareness of the server half.

questions.q: What makes a modal dialog accessible?
choices: A high z-index and a dark overlay, so it is visually on top
Rendering it in a portal, so it sits at the end of the body
Setting `aria-hidden` on the modal until it has fully opened
Focus moves in and stays inside, Escape closes it, and it is labelled
questions.why: It also needs `role="dialog"`, an inert background, and focus returned to the opener on close. A portal fixes stacking and overflow, not accessibility: tab order follows the DOM, so you still have to trap focus inside the dialog yourself.
questions.asked: A strong mid-level signal: most candidates only mention the overlay.

questions.q: What is a portal for?
choices: Loading a component's code lazily the first time it is shown
Rendering a component on the server and streaming it to the client
Rendering into a DOM node elsewhere, while keeping React context
Sharing state between two routes without lifting it to the root
questions.why: It escapes `overflow: hidden` and z-index stacking for modals, tooltips and toasts. Context still flows and synthetic events still bubble through the React tree, which surprises people expecting DOM behaviour.
questions.asked: It usually leads into 'so where do events from a portal bubble?'.

questions.q: Why put a table's filters in the URL query string?
choices: Reading the URL is faster than reading component state
The view can be shared, bookmarked, refreshed and navigated back to
It reduces re-renders, because the router batches the updates
The server requires filters in the URL so it can cache the responses
questions.why: 'Send me that filtered view' is a real user need, and back/forward come free. The rule of thumb: state that describes what you are looking at belongs in the URL. It is not a performance technique.
questions.asked: A design question that shows product sense as well as React knowledge.

questions.q: What does list virtualisation do?
choices: Mounts only the rows in view plus a buffer, whatever the list length
Loads the next page of data from the API as the user scrolls down
Caches every rendered row in memory so scrolling back is instant
Compresses the list data so that it takes less memory in the browser
questions.why: 10,000 rows means 10,000 DOM nodes and a frozen page; virtualising keeps about 30 mounted. Loading more data is infinite scroll, a separate concern. The costs: variable row heights are hard, and Ctrl-F stops finding off-screen rows.
questions.asked: The standard answer to 'this table with 10,000 rows is slow'.

questions.q: From an engineering view, how does infinite scroll differ from numbered pagination?
choices: They are the same data fetching, only styled differently in the UI
Infinite scroll is always faster, because it never refetches data
It needs cursor paging and accumulated state; pages can use offsets
Pagination must be server-side, while infinite scroll is client-only
questions.why: Offset paging over a live dataset duplicates or skips rows as items are inserted, which shows up badly when pages are appended. Infinite scroll also hides the footer, loses the scroll position on back navigation, and needs a keyboard-accessible alternative.
questions.asked: A product-engineering question: the strong answer names the data problem and the UX costs.

questions.q: How do you make a component work both controlled and uncontrolled?
choices: Use internal state only when the optional `value` prop is undefined
Keep internal state always, and sync the `value` prop in with an effect
Export two separate components, one controlled and one uncontrolled
Keep the value in a ref in both cases and read it on each change
questions.why: This 'controllable' pattern is used by every component library: `const isControlled = value !== undefined`. Syncing a prop into state with an effect gives two sources of truth and a render of lag.
questions.asked: It separates people who have built reusable components from people who have only consumed them.

questions.q: What is the keyboard contract for a dropdown menu?
choices: Tab moves between the items, and Enter selects the currently focused item
Only mouse interaction is needed, as long as there is a label
Space opens each submenu, and Tab moves between the submenus
Arrows move between items, Enter selects, Escape closes, Tab leaves
questions.why: Roving tabindex: the menu is one tab stop and arrows move within it. Making every item tabbable is the common mistake: it forces a keyboard user through 40 stops to get past your menu.
questions.asked: It checks whether you have built an accessible widget rather than only a styled one.

questions.q: What should a good component test assert on?
choices: A snapshot of every component's full rendered output
What the user sees and does: text, roles and interactions
The values of each hook's internal state after each action
Nothing at unit level: only end-to-end tests are reliable
questions.why: Tests coupled to implementation break on every refactor and let real bugs through. Querying by role also catches accessibility problems for free. Snapshots of everything turn into approval noise nobody reads.
questions.asked: The Testing Library philosophy question; expect it for any React role that mentions tests.

questions.q: What is wrong with this line?
questions.code: const [value, setValue] = useState(props.value);
choices: `useState` cannot take a prop as its initial value
It reads the prop only once, so later changes are ignored
It causes an infinite loop when `props.value` changes
It copies the prop by reference, so edits mutate the parent
questions.why: `useState`'s argument is only the initial value. If you meant 'reset when the prop changes', change the key; if you meant a default, name the prop `defaultValue` so the one-shot behaviour is documented.
questions.asked: A common review comment; the strong answer offers both fixes and says when each applies.

questions.q: You are asked to make a slow page faster. What do you do first?
choices: Wrap the heavier components in `React.memo`
Add `useMemo` around the costly-looking calculations
Split the bundle so less JavaScript loads at startup
Profile it to see what re-renders and for how long
questions.why: The React Profiler tells you which component, how often and how long. Optimising by guesswork usually adds complexity, moves nothing, and sometimes makes it slower.
questions.asked: Whether you measure before optimising is one of the clearest seniority signals there is.

questions.q: What is code splitting in a React app?
choices: Loading route or feature bundles on demand with `lazy` and Suspense
Splitting large components into several smaller source files
Separating the CSS from the JavaScript into different bundles
Running independent components in parallel on separate threads
questions.why: The usual first cut is per route. Watch for a waterfall: lazy-loading a component that then fetches its own data serialises two round trips. File structure alone changes nothing about what the browser downloads.
questions.asked: The first answer to 'our bundle is 3 MB', and the waterfall follow-up shows depth.

questions.q: What does a router give you beyond swapping components on screen?
choices: Faster rendering, because routes are compiled ahead of time
Server-side rendering of every route with no extra configuration
URL state, back and forward, deep links, and per-route loading
Automatic authentication checks on every route it matches
questions.why: The URL becomes state the browser understands, so history and links work. Per route, it can also start data loading before the component renders and split the code so each route downloads only what it needs. Authentication is still something you wire in.
questions.asked: It checks you can justify the dependency, not just that you have used one.

questions.q: When is a global client-state store justified over context plus local state?
choices: As soon as two components anywhere in the app share one value
For any app with more than about ten components in its tree
Never: context plus local state always scales far enough
When many unrelated components read and write shared state often
questions.why: Much of what used to go in Redux is server cache, which a data-fetching library handles better. What remains (session, UI shell, cross-cutting toggles) is often small enough for context, until frequent updates from many places make re-render scope matter.
questions.asked: Distinguishing server state from client state is the strong move.

questions.q: What is the risk of `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`?
choices: It is slow, because React re-parses the HTML on every render
It breaks the virtual DOM diff for every sibling of the element
It inserts raw HTML, so unsanitised content becomes an XSS hole
It only works in development builds and is stripped in production
questions.why: React escapes interpolated values by default, which is why XSS is rare in React apps; this prop is the explicit opt-out. Sanitise with a library such as DOMPurify, and never pass raw user input.
questions.asked: A quick security filter for any frontend role that renders user content.

questions.q: What undo/redo approach does immutable state make almost free?
choices: Re-fetching the previous version of the data from the server
Keeping past, present and future stacks of state snapshots
Storing the last value in a ref and restoring it on undo
Recording DOM mutations and replaying them in reverse
questions.why: With immutable updates each state is a snapshot you can keep without copying, so undo is moving entries between stacks. Diff-based designs (command pattern, Immer patches) also work but need more code. It is the strongest practical argument for not mutating state.
questions.asked: It links immutability to a feature users want, which is how interviewers test if the principle stuck.

questions.q:
In `

Title

`, what does `Card` receive as `children`?
choices: The `<h2>` element, to place wherever it likes
The string `'Title'`, with the tag stripped off
Nothing: `Card` must read its own DOM children
An array holding a single rendered DOM node
questions.why: Anything between a component's tags arrives as `props.children`, here a React element, not a DOM node. `Card` decides where to render it, which is how layout components wrap content they know nothing about.
questions.asked: The basis of composition; everything from layouts to compound components builds on it.

questions.q: What is a render prop?
choices: A boolean prop that decides whether a component renders at all
A prop that holds pre-rendered HTML as a string to be inserted
A function prop the component calls to render, passing it data
A prop that forces a child to re-render when its value changes
questions.why: `<List items={users} renderItem={(u) => <UserRow user={u} />} />` lets the component own the looping or the logic while the caller owns the markup. Hooks replaced many render props for sharing logic, but they remain common for customising what a component draws.
questions.asked: It checks you can read older library APIs and know when the pattern still fits.

questions.q: Why did hooks replace most higher-order components (HOCs)?
choices: Hooks share logic without wrappers, avoiding hidden or clashing props
HOCs stopped working with function components after React 16.8
Hooks run faster, because HOCs force an extra render on every update
HOCs cannot pass props down, so each one needed its own context
questions.why: Stacking `withRouter(withAuth(withTheme(Page)))` produced wrapper hell, props injected from nowhere, and name collisions between HOCs. A hook call makes the dependency explicit in the component body. HOCs still work; they are just rarely the best tool now.
questions.asked: Older codebases are full of HOCs; this checks you can maintain them and explain the move away.

questions.q: What is the container/presentational split?
choices: Putting every component inside a CSS container for layout
Class components hold the state; function components hold the UI
Wrapping pages in a container that catches errors from children
One component loads and manages data; another only renders props
questions.why: The presentational component is easy to test and reuse because it only turns props into markup; the container deals with fetching and state. Hooks made the split less rigid, but keeping data access out of reusable UI is still good practice.
questions.asked: It shows whether you think about where data access belongs in a component tree.

questions.q: What is this pattern called, and what does it give `Layout`?
questions.code:
<Layout
  header={<Nav />}
  sidebar={<Filters />}
>
  <Results />
</Layout>
choices: Render props: `Layout` calls each prop to get its markup
Slot props: named places for content `Layout` knows nothing of
Compound components: they share state with `Layout` implicitly
Higher-order components: each prop wraps `Layout` in a new layer
questions.why: Elements passed as named props work like extra `children`: `Layout` only decides where they go. The parent keeps ownership of their props and state, so no drilling is needed. They are elements, not functions, which is what distinguishes them from render props.
questions.asked: Slots are the composition answer to prop drilling, and interviewers like candidates who reach for them.

questions.q: This edit form mounts while `user` is still loading, then stays empty. Which fix also keeps the user's edits when the data refetches in the background?
choices: Copy `user` into state in an effect that depends on `user`
Render the form only once `data` exists, keyed by `data.id`
Copy `user.name` into state during render whenever the `user` object changes
Pass `user.name` as the input's `value` with no local state
questions.why: Mounting after load gives `useState` the real initial value, and keying by id resets the form only for a different user. A refetch returns a new object with the same id, so edits survive; the effect and the render-time copy both fire on the new object reference and overwrite them. Without local state the input cannot be edited.
questions.asked: Every CRUD app has an edit screen; this is the bug they all hit first.

questions.q: Users delete emails often and occasionally by mistake. Which delete UX serves them best?
choices: A confirm dialog on every delete, so mistakes are always caught
Disable delete for items the user has opened in the last hour
Require the user to type the item's name before each delete
Delete at once and offer Undo in a toast for a few seconds
questions.why: Frequent confirm dialogs get clicked through by habit, so they add friction without catching mistakes. Undo keeps the common case fast and makes the rare mistake cheap. Typed confirmation suits rare, irreversible actions such as deleting a whole project.
questions.asked: A product-sense question; strong candidates match the safeguard to how often and how reversible the action is.

questions.q: When is a skeleton screen better than a spinner?
choices: When the layout of the incoming content is known in advance
When the request usually takes under 100 ms to return
When the request might fail and needs a retry button
When the page is rendered on the server, never the client
questions.why: A skeleton reserves the shape of the content, so the page does not jump when data arrives and the wait feels shorter. For very fast responses, showing nothing for a moment avoids a flash of either.
questions.asked: It shows attention to perceived performance and layout shift, which users notice.

questions.q: Why do larger React codebases group files by feature rather than by type, such as `components/` and `hooks/`?
choices: Bundlers can only code-split folders that contain a whole feature
React requires a component's custom hooks to live in the same folder as the component
Code that changes together lives together, so a feature is easy to find and delete
Grouping by type causes circular imports that break hot module reloading
questions.why: A change to 'invoices' then touches one folder instead of five, and removing a feature is deleting a directory. Bundlers split on dynamic imports, not folders, and React has no rule about file layout.
questions.asked: It checks whether you have worked in a codebase big enough for structure to matter.

questions.q: What is the main cost of a polymorphic `as` prop, as in `<Button as="a" href="/x">`?
choices: It forces a remount whenever the `as` value changes between renders
React cannot render a tag name that arrives as a string prop
It removes the element from the accessibility tree entirely
Typing it well is hard, since the allowed props must follow `as`
questions.why: `href` is valid only when `as="a"`, so correct types need generics over the element type; naive versions accept invalid combinations or lose autocomplete. React renders string tag names fine. The pattern is worth it in design systems, less so in app code.
questions.asked: It probes design-system experience and TypeScript depth at the same time.

questions.q: In React 19, a click lands on a button rendered through `createPortal` into `document.body`. The component that rendered the portal sits inside a `<div onClick={log}>`. Does `log` run?
choices: No, because the button is not a DOM descendant of the div
Yes, because React events bubble along the component tree
Only if the portal target has `onClick` wired up to forward it
Only for capture listeners such as `onClickCapture` on the div
questions.why: React dispatches synthetic events along the React tree, so a portal child still bubbles to its React ancestors even though its DOM node lives elsewhere. That is why a click inside a portalled modal can trigger an "outside click" handler on a parent unless you stop propagation or check the target.
questions.asked: It catches people who built a modal with a portal and then chased a mystery "click outside closes it" bug.

questions.q: What does `useContext(ThemeContext)` return when no `ThemeContext` provider exists above the component?
questions.code: const ThemeContext = createContext('light');
choices: It throws, because context must always have a provider above it
`undefined`, because `'light'` is only used for type inference
`'light'`, the default value passed to `createContext`
The value from the nearest provider of any context in the tree
questions.why: The argument to `createContext` is the fallback used when no provider is found. Many teams pass `null` and have a custom hook throw a clear error instead, so a missing provider fails loudly rather than silently using a default.
questions.asked: Leads straight into the follow-up: how do you make a missing provider fail loudly?

questions.q: Why do many codebases wrap `useContext` in a custom hook like this?
choices: A missing provider fails at once with a message naming the fix
The hook caches the context value so consumers render less often
Custom hooks let context be read from inside class components too
It stops the context value from being read outside of rendering
questions.why: With a `null` default and a guard, forgetting the provider becomes a clear error at the call site, and TypeScript narrows the return type to non-null. The hook adds no caching: consumers still re-render whenever the provided value changes.
questions.asked: Shows you have wired context into a real codebase rather than only read the docs.

questions.q: In React 19, which of these renders a provider for `ThemeContext`?
choices: <ThemeContext.Consumer value="dark">{children}</ThemeContext.Consumer>
<ThemeContext value="dark">{children}</ThemeContext>
<Provider context={ThemeContext} value="dark">{children}</Provider>
<ThemeContext.Root value="dark">{children}</ThemeContext.Root>
questions.why: React 19 lets you render the context object itself as the provider; `<ThemeContext.Provider>` still works but is on the path to deprecation. `Consumer` reads a value rather than providing one, and there is no generic `Provider` component or `.Root` in React.
questions.asked: A quick check that you have kept up with React 19 syntax you will meet in code review.

questions.q: In React 19, what can `use(ThemeContext)` do that `useContext(ThemeContext)` cannot?
choices: Subscribe to only one field of the context value, skipping other changes
Read the context without a provider, ignoring the default value passed
Be called inside a condition or loop, not only at the top of a component
Read context in an event handler after the component has finished rendering
questions.why: `use` is the one hook-like API allowed inside `if` blocks and loops, so you can read context only on the branch that needs it. It still re-renders on any change to the value, still uses the default without a provider, and like every hook it runs during render, not in handlers.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see whether you know `use` is special-cased, not just a rename.

questions.q: A single `AppContext` holds `{ user, theme, cart }`. Adding an item to the cart makes the header, the sidebar and the settings page re-render. What is the most direct fix?
choices: Wrap every consumer in `React.memo` so context changes are skipped
Split it into contexts so each consumer subscribes to one concern
Move the provider lower so fewer components can read the cart
Store the cart in a ref so updating it never triggers a render
questions.why: Every consumer of a context re-renders when its value changes, and `memo` does not block context updates. Splitting by concern (and by update frequency) means cart changes only reach cart consumers. A ref would stop the badge from ever updating at all.
questions.asked: The classic follow-up to "when would you use context?"; strong candidates mention update frequency as the split line.

questions.q: Why do some providers expose the state and the dispatch function through two separate contexts?
questions.code:
<CountStateContext value={count}>
  <CountDispatchContext value={dispatch}>
    {children}
  </CountDispatchContext>
</CountStateContext>
choices: React only lets one value be provided per context, so both need a slot
Dispatch has to be provided above the state to be read from reducers
Components that only dispatch do not re-render when the state changes
It lets the state be read in class components and dispatch in hooks
questions.why: `dispatch` from `useReducer` is stable, so a context holding only it never changes and its consumers (buttons, forms) are not re-rendered by state updates. One context holding both would change on every state update. A context value can be any object, so one slot is not the reason.
questions.asked: It shows you understand what actually triggers context re-renders and how to design around it.

questions.q: A context value changes 60 times a second (a mouse position). What is the usual problem, and the usual fix?
choices: Every consumer re-renders each frame; use local state or a store with selectors
The context drops updates after 16 ms; switch to a ref and a forced render instead
React batches the updates away; wrap each change in `flushSync` so none are lost
The provider remounts its children each time; add a stable `key` to the provider
questions.why: Context has no selectors, so every consumer re-renders on every change, even if it only needs a derived value. High-frequency values belong in local state near their only user, or in an external store (Zustand, `useSyncExternalStore`) where components subscribe to the slice they need.
questions.asked: Checks that you know context is dependency injection, not a general-purpose fast-changing store.

questions.q: What is the "slot" pattern in component design?
questions.code:
<PageLayout
  header={<Breadcrumbs />}
  sidebar={<Filters />}
>
  <OrdersTable />
</PageLayout>
choices: Passing a list of component names that the layout imports lazily
Letting the layout clone each child and inject its own props into it
Registering children with the layout through a context in an effect
Passing elements as named props so the layout places them itself
questions.why: Elements are values, so any prop can carry one; the layout decides where each slot goes while the caller decides what fills it. It avoids prop drilling for the pieces and needs no cloning or registration. `children` is simply the default slot.
questions.asked: A composition-first answer to layout questions is what separates mid-level from junior React code.

questions.q: A `Tabs` component uses `React.Children.map` and `cloneElement` to pass `isActive` to each `Tab`. A teammate wraps one tab in a component called `PermissionGate`. What breaks?
choices: `Children.map` throws, because it cannot iterate over custom components
The prop lands on `PermissionGate`, so the inner tab never gets it
Keys are lost, so every tab remounts and loses state on each render
Nothing breaks, because `cloneElement` recurses into nested children
questions.why: `cloneElement` only touches the direct children it is given, so any wrapper swallows the injected props. Compound components that share state through context keep working no matter how deeply the parts are nested, which is why they have replaced cloning.
questions.asked: Shows you know why modern compound components use context instead of `cloneElement`.

questions.q: What is a "headless" component library (for example Radix Primitives, React Aria or Headless UI)?
choices: A library that renders components on the server without a browser
Components that ship behaviour and accessibility but no styles
Components that render without a root DOM element of their own
A library of hooks that only works in apps without a design system
questions.why: Headless components handle the hard parts (focus management, keyboard support, ARIA state) and leave styling to you, so they fit any design system. shadcn/ui is a popular set of styled components built on top of such primitives.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that you would not hand-roll a combobox when an accessible primitive exists.

questions.q: What does the "prop getter" pattern give a hook-based component like `useCombobox`?
questions.code:
const { getInputProps, getItemProps } = useCombobox({ items });
<input {...getInputProps({ onBlur: track })} />
choices: The hook reads props from the input so it no longer needs its own state
It lets the hook replace the element with a custom one after rendering
It merges the caller's handlers with the ARIA and event wiring the hook needs
It memoises each prop object so the input skips re-rendering on typing
questions.why: The getter returns every attribute the element needs (`role`, `aria-*`, `id`, handlers) and composes in the caller's own props, so passing `onBlur` does not overwrite the hook's handler. It is about correct merging, not memoisation.
questions.asked: A strong answer names the bug it prevents: a caller's handler silently replacing the library's.

questions.q: A `Button` wrapper spreads unknown props onto the native element. Why put `{...rest}` before your own handler here?
choices: Later props win, so the tracking handler is never overwritten
JSX requires spreads to come first, before any explicitly named attributes
Props spread last are ignored by React when they duplicate a named prop
It makes TypeScript infer the button element type for the rest object
questions.why: In JSX, later attributes override earlier ones, exactly like object spread. Putting `{...rest}` first means your composed handler wins, and because `onClick` was destructured out it is called inside it rather than overwriting it. Spreads may go anywhere in JSX.
questions.asked: Order of spread vs explicit props is a frequent code review comment on shared components.

questions.q: What is the `asChild` (Slot) pattern used by libraries such as Radix?
questions.code: Help
choices: The trigger renders both its own button and the link as siblings
The child is rendered in a portal so the tooltip can position it
The link is converted into a button so it can receive focus
The trigger merges its props and ref into the child element
questions.why: With `asChild`, the component renders no element of its own and clones its behaviour (handlers, ARIA, ref) onto the single child, so you avoid a `<button>` wrapping an `<a>`, which is invalid interactive nesting. It is an alternative to a polymorphic `as` prop.
questions.asked: Shows familiarity with the component libraries most teams actually use in 2026.

questions.q: A `DataTable` has grown 31 boolean props like `showFooter`, `compact`, `hideSearch`. Which refactor does a senior reviewer usually suggest?
choices: Group the booleans into one `options` object prop with the same keys
Move the flags into a context so callers do not have to pass them
Split it into parts the caller composes, like `<Table.Search />`
Replace the flags with a single `variant` string covering each combination
questions.why: Boolean props multiply combinations the component must handle and test. Composition lets callers include only the parts they need and keeps each part simple. An options object or context just moves the same flags around, and one variant per combination explodes.
questions.asked: Tests whether you recognise "boolean prop explosion" and reach for composition.

questions.q: What does `key={user.id}` on this form achieve?
questions.code: <EditUserForm key={user.id} user={user} />
choices: Each user gets a fresh form, so leftover edits do not carry over
It lets React reuse the same form DOM nodes for faster switching
It memoises the form so it only re-renders when the user id changes
It tells React to keep draft state per user and restore it on return
questions.why: A different key makes React unmount the old instance and mount a new one, so `useState(user.name)` initialisers run again. It does the opposite of reuse and does not store old drafts; switching back mounts yet another fresh form.
questions.asked: It is the idiomatic answer to "how do you reset a form when the selected record changes?".

questions.q: What is an "inversion of control" API like this for?
choices: It lets the hook dispatch actions to other hooks in the same component
Callers can change state transitions without forking the hook
It moves state out of React so the hook can run in a web worker
It lets a parent read the hook's state without it being lifted
questions.why: The "state reducer" pattern hands the transition logic to the caller, who can override specific actions and delegate the rest to the default reducer. It is how reusable hooks cover edge cases without adding a new option for each one.
questions.asked: Appears when discussing reusable component libraries; it signals you have designed APIs for other developers.

questions.q: In a React app, what is a "custom hook" boundary most useful for?
choices: Sharing state between components, since each call returns the same state
Making code run faster by moving it outside the component body
Naming and hiding a piece of stateful logic so components read clearly
Avoiding re-renders, because updates inside a hook do not affect callers
questions.why: A custom hook extracts logic, not state: each call gets its own state, and updates inside it re-render the calling component as usual. The win is readability and reuse (`useDebouncedValue`, `useOrders`), plus a seam you can test with `renderHook`.
questions.asked: The misconception that hooks share state between callers is common; interviewers probe for it.

questions.q: Two components each call `useCart()`, which is `useState([])` inside. One adds an item. What does the other see?
choices: The new item, because both calls read the same hook instance
The new item after its next render, once React syncs the hooks
An error, because a custom hook can only be used in one place
Nothing new, because each call owns separate state
questions.why: Hooks share logic, not state: every call site gets its own `useState` slot. To share the cart you lift the state to a common parent, put it in context, or use an external store.
questions.asked: A quick filter for whether a candidate has a correct mental model of hooks.

questions.q: Which statement about the container/presentational split is most accurate in a 2026 React codebase?
choices: It is required, because hooks cannot be used in presentational components
It is replaced by custom hooks, yet still useful for Storybook and tests
It is obsolete, because Server Components forbid presentational components
It is mandatory for performance, because containers skip re-renders
questions.why: Hooks let a component own its data logic directly, so strict containers are rarely needed. The idea survives where it pays: a pure view that takes props is trivial to render in Storybook or a test, with a thin wrapper doing the fetching.
questions.asked: Interviewers look for a nuanced answer: you know the pattern and when it still earns its keep.

questions.q: What does this generic `List` component gain from the `renderItem` prop?
choices: The list owns markup and keys; the caller owns how an item looks
Items render lazily, so only the visible part of the list is rendered
The list can skip rendering items whose data has not changed since last time
The caller can reorder items without the list having to know their ids
questions.why: A render prop is inversion of control over rendering: `List` owns structure and keys, the caller owns item presentation. It does nothing for laziness or memoisation; virtualisation needs a windowing library.
questions.asked: Checks you can explain a render prop by what it decouples, not only by its syntax.

questions.q: You need the same "confirm before delete" behaviour on six buttons across the app. Which design keeps it most reusable?
choices: A higher-order component that wraps every page and intercepts all clicks
A global `window.confirm` override installed once in `main.jsx`
A context flag each delete handler checks before calling the API
A `useConfirm()` hook that opens one shared dialog and returns a promise
questions.why: A promise-returning `useConfirm` (backed by one dialog rendered near the root) lets any handler write `if (await confirm("Delete?")) remove()`. It keeps the flow linear and the dialog accessible. A page-wide HOC or a global override is invasive and hard to reason about.
questions.asked: A design question that reveals whether you think in terms of reusable hooks and single shared UI.

questions.q: In a compound `Accordion`, each `Accordion.Item` needs to know whether it is open. How should it get that?
choices: From a context the `Accordion` root provides, read with a hook
From `cloneElement`, with the root injecting `isOpen` into each item
From a module-level variable shared by the root and every item
From the DOM, by reading `aria-expanded` on the item's own button
questions.why: Context lets any descendant read the shared state regardless of nesting, and a module variable would be shared across every accordion on the page. Reading ARIA attributes back from the DOM inverts the data flow; the DOM should reflect state, not hold it.
questions.asked: Expected follow-up after "what are compound components?": how do the parts talk to each other?

questions.q: Why is defining a component inside another component's body a bug?
choices: Inner components cannot use hooks, because they are not at the top level
React warns and falls back to rendering the inner function as plain markup
Each render makes a new `Row` type, so every row remounts
Inner components cannot receive a `key`, so the list order becomes unstable
questions.why: Component identity is the function reference. A new function per render means a new type, so React tears down the old subtree and mounts a new one: inputs lose focus and state resets. Move `Row` to module scope and pass what it needs as props.
questions.asked: A common real bug; strong candidates explain it in terms of element type identity.

questions.q: A modal needs to close when the user clicks outside it. Which approach avoids the usual bugs?
choices: Listen for `click` on `window` and close whenever `e.target` is not the dialog
Stop propagation on every click inside the modal so the window never sees them
Close on backdrop `mousedown` only if the pointer went down on the backdrop itself
Use a `blur` handler on the dialog, because focus leaving means a click outside
questions.why: Checking that the press started on the backdrop avoids closing when a text selection drag ends outside. Comparing `e.target` fails for clicks on children, blanket `stopPropagation` breaks other listeners, and `blur` fires on tabbing too. A native `<dialog>` with `closedby="any"` handles this for you where supported.
questions.asked: Real-world modal bugs are a favourite senior probe; this one separates people who have shipped one.

questions.q: You build a component library. Why accept `className` and merge it rather than ignore it?
choices: React warns about unknown props unless `className` is always passed along
Callers can adjust layout such as margins without forking the component
Merged class names are required for server rendering to hydrate correctly
Class names are the only way to pass a ref through a function component
questions.why: Layout concerns like spacing belong to the parent, so a reusable component should accept and merge `className` (often with `clsx` plus `tailwind-merge`). It has nothing to do with refs or hydration, and React does not warn about a missing `className`.
questions.asked: Small detail, but it shows you have built components other people consume.

questions.q: In React 19, how does a function component expose its inner `<input>` DOM node to a parent that passes `ref`?
choices: It cannot; the component must still be wrapped in `forwardRef`
It reads `ref` as a prop and attaches it to the input, as shown
The parent gets the `<label>`, because refs attach to the root element
React attaches the ref to the first focusable descendant automatically
questions.why: Since React 19, `ref` is a normal prop for function components, so `forwardRef` is no longer needed for new code. You put it on whichever element the parent should get; React does not guess.
questions.asked: Checks that you have written React 19 code, not only React 18.

questions.q: A parent keeps `isOpen` for a `Disclosure` and passes `open`/`onOpenChange`. Which name pair is the conventional API for a controlled component?
choices: `defaultOpen` with `setOpen`, mirroring the `useState` return value
`open` with `onOpenChange`, plus `defaultOpen` for the uncontrolled case
`isOpen` with `toggle`, so the child can flip the value directly
`initialOpen` with `onClose`, so the parent only hears about closing
questions.why: Libraries such as Radix follow the native pattern: `value`/`onChange` for controlled use and `defaultValue` for uncontrolled. `onOpenChange` reports the requested new value, so the parent stays the owner. A child-owned `toggle` would hide the state transition.
questions.asked: API naming consistency is a signal of experience with shared component libraries.

questions.q: In a component library, why should a controlled component never also copy its `value` prop into its own state?
choices: It doubles the renders, but otherwise behaves exactly like the prop
It breaks the rules of hooks, because props cannot seed `useState`
State initialised from props is reset on every render of the parent
Once the parent changes or rejects `value`, the copy no longer follows it
questions.why: `useState(value)` only reads `value` on mount. If the parent resets the rating or refuses a change, the component keeps showing its own copy: two sources of truth. A controlled component should render straight from the prop.
questions.asked: "Mirroring props in state" is one of the most common review comments; interviewers want the two-sources-of-truth explanation.

questions.q: What does wrapping part of a page in `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` do?
choices: Shows the fallback while anything inside suspends, e.g. a lazy import
Delays rendering of the children until all effects inside them have run
Catches errors from the children and shows the fallback instead of them
Renders the children on the server only, with the fallback on the client
questions.why: Suspense shows its fallback while a descendant is waiting on something that suspends: a `lazy()` component, `use(promise)`, or a Suspense-enabled data library. Errors are the job of error boundaries, which are a separate mechanism.
questions.asked: People mix up Suspense and error boundaries; this checks you keep them apart.

questions.q: A dashboard has four widgets that load independently. Why wrap each in its own `<Suspense>` rather than one around the page?
choices: React only allows one suspended component per Suspense boundary
Each widget appears as soon as it is ready instead of waiting for the slowest
Separate boundaries make the four requests run in parallel instead of in series
Nested boundaries let the server stream HTML, which one boundary blocks
questions.why: A boundary shows its fallback until everything inside it is ready, so one boundary means the whole page waits for the slowest widget. Boundaries control what is revealed together; they do not decide whether requests run in parallel, which depends on when the fetches start.
questions.asked: Boundary placement is a design decision; interviewers want to hear "what should appear together?".

questions.q: Why is a `useEffect` that fetches in every widget a common source of request waterfalls?
choices: Effects run in series, so each widget waits for the previous effect to finish
Browsers cap fetches started from effects at one per origin at a time
Effects run after render, so children fetch after parents finish loading
An effect cannot start a fetch until the component has hydrated twice
questions.why: When a child only renders after its parent's data arrives, its own effect fetch starts late, giving parent-then-child sequential requests. Route loaders, a query library's prefetching, or starting fetches higher up let them run in parallel. Effects themselves are not serialised.
questions.asked: Understanding why fetch-in-effect produces waterfalls is the reason route loaders and query libraries exist.

questions.q: Why does `Card` still re-render every time `App` re-renders?
choices: `memo` never applies to components that render `children`
`<span>` is a new element object each render
State updates in a parent always bypass `memo` on its direct children
`memo` compares props deeply, and the span has no stable key
questions.why: JSX compiles to a fresh element object each time `App` renders, so the `children` prop is a new reference and the shallow comparison fails. `memo` does work with children if you hoist the element or memoise it; the comparison is shallow, not deep.
questions.asked: A favourite trick question: it checks whether you know `memo` compares prop references, and JSX is always a new object.

questions.q: A `ThemeProvider` holds theme state and renders `{children}`. When the theme changes, which components re-render?
choices: Every component inside the provider, since the provider re-rendered
Only components that read `ThemeContext`
Only the direct children passed in `children`
None until the parent of the provider also re-renders
questions.why: The `children` elements were created by the provider's parent, which did not re-render, so React sees the same element references and skips them. Only context consumers update. This is why providers take `children` rather than rendering the app tree themselves.
questions.asked: Explaining why the children-as-props provider is cheap shows a real understanding of how React decides to re-render.

questions.q: What does the React DevTools Profiler record?
choices: Each network request and the component that started it
Each commit, with render time per component
The size of each component in the production JavaScript bundle
Memory used by each component, sampled once per second
questions.why: The Profiler records commits and shows a flame graph and ranked chart of render durations, and with "record why each component rendered" enabled it tells you which props, state or hooks changed. Network and memory are the browser DevTools' jobs.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that you measure before you memoise.

questions.q: The Profiler shows `ProductGrid` re-rendering on every keystroke in an unrelated search box. What is the first thing to check?
choices: Whether `ProductGrid` has too many DOM nodes to render quickly
Whether the search state lives above `ProductGrid`
Whether the browser is throttling the page's main thread
Whether `ProductGrid` is missing a `key` prop at its call site
questions.why: A component re-renders when an ancestor does, so search state held too high drags the grid along. Moving the state down into the search component (colocation) is usually the fix before any `memo`. DOM size affects how slow each render is, not why it happens.
questions.asked: State placement is the cheapest performance fix; a strong answer reaches for it before memoisation.

questions.q: In a `<Profiler onRender>` callback, what is the difference between `actualDuration` and `baseDuration`?
choices: Actual is time in the browser; base is time spent in React code only
Actual is for the first mount; base is the average of later updates
Actual is this commit's render time; base estimates rendering all without memo
Actual includes effects; base covers render time up to the commit
questions.why: `actualDuration` measures time spent rendering the profiled subtree for this commit, so it drops when memoisation skips work. `baseDuration` estimates the cost of re-rendering the whole subtree from scratch. Comparing them tells you how much memoisation is saving.
questions.asked: Rarely asked directly, but knowing it shows you have used the Profiler API rather than guessed.

questions.q: Why should you profile React performance with a production build rather than `npm run dev`?
choices: Dev builds add checks and Strict Mode double renders
The Profiler tab is disabled in development to avoid slowing hot reload
Development builds skip memoisation, so `memo` has no effect there
Production builds are the only ones that include component names
questions.why: Development React runs extra warnings and validation, and Strict Mode renders twice, so absolute numbers are misleading. Use a profiling-enabled production build to measure real cost. Memoisation works in both; dev builds actually keep more names.
questions.asked: A practical detail that tells interviewers you have actually chased a performance problem.

questions.q: When does `useCallback` on a handler actually save work?
choices: Always, because creating a new function on each render is expensive
When it is passed to a `memo` child or used in an effect's dependencies
When the handler is attached to a native element such as a `<button>`
When the handler calls `setState`, because React batches it better
questions.why: A stable function only matters to something that compares it: a memoised child's props or a dependency array. Creating functions is cheap, and native elements do not care about handler identity. Without such a consumer, `useCallback` is pure overhead.
questions.asked: Tests whether you memoise by habit or for a reason you can state.

questions.q: What does the React Compiler (v1, 2025) do for a typical app?
choices: It converts class components to function components during the build
It moves rendering into a web worker so the main thread stays free
It compiles JSX to direct DOM calls so React no longer needs a virtual DOM
It memoises components and values at build time, as manual `useMemo` would
questions.why: The compiler analyses components and hooks and inserts fine-grained memoisation automatically, which makes most hand-written `useMemo`, `useCallback` and `memo` unnecessary. It relies on your code following the Rules of React and skips functions it cannot prove safe.
questions.asked: Current-knowledge check: interviewers ask how the compiler changes memoisation advice.

questions.q: The React Compiler is enabled, but one component mutates a prop during render. What happens?
choices: The build fails until the mutation is removed from the component
The compiler copies the prop first so the mutation becomes safe
It may skip optimising that component, which then runs as before
The component is memoised anyway and may show stale values
questions.why: The compiler assumes the Rules of React (pure render, no mutation of props or state). When it detects a violation it bails out of that function and leaves it unoptimised; the lint rules report the problem. It does not rewrite your logic.
questions.asked: Shows you know the compiler is not magic: it depends on pure components.

questions.q: What does list virtualisation cost you, in exchange for rendering only visible rows?
choices: Browser find-in-page cannot see rows that are not rendered
Rows can no longer hold their own local state or effects
The list cannot be sorted without re-fetching all its data
Keyboard focus stops working inside any virtualised row
questions.why: Off-screen rows do not exist in the DOM, so Ctrl+F, screen readers counting rows, and printing all see only the window; you also need known or measured heights. Rows keep state while mounted, and sorting is a data concern.
questions.asked: A good answer weighs the trade-off rather than treating virtualisation as free.

questions.q: A table shows 50 rows per page from a paginated API. A teammate proposes virtualising it. What is the best response?
choices: Agree, because virtualisation always improves scroll performance
Agree, but only if every row has a fixed height in CSS
Disagree, because virtualisation breaks server-side pagination
Decline: 50 rows are cheap, so measure first and keep it simple
questions.why: Virtualisation pays off with hundreds or thousands of rows or heavy row components. At 50 rows the added complexity, accessibility caveats and scroll quirks cost more than they save. Libraries like TanStack Virtual handle variable heights too, so that is not the deciding factor.
questions.asked: Interviewers like candidates who push back on premature optimisation with a reason.

questions.q: Why does this lazy component remount and flash its fallback on every render of `Page`?
choices: `lazy` must be wrapped in `useMemo` or it re-downloads the module
`import()` is not cached, so each call fetches the chunk again
Each render creates a new `lazy` component type
`Suspense` must sit outside `Page` for the fallback to be skipped
questions.why: Every call to `lazy` returns a new component type, so React treats it as a different component each render, unmounts the old one and suspends again. The module itself is cached by the bundler; the problem is identity. Declare lazy components at the top level of the module.
questions.asked: A real bug that looks innocent; it tests your grasp of component identity.

questions.q: How can you make a lazily loaded `SettingsPanel` open without a visible loading delay?
questions.code:
const loadSettings = () => import("./SettingsPanel");
const SettingsPanel = lazy(loadSettings);
choices: Call `loadSettings()` on hover or focus of the button
Wrap `SettingsPanel` in `memo` so its chunk stays in memory
Add `loading="eager"` to the `<Suspense>` around the panel
Render it in a hidden `<div>` on mount so it is always present
questions.why: Calling the same `import()` early starts downloading the chunk; the promise is cached, so when `lazy` later calls it the module is ready. Rendering it hidden defeats the split, and `memo` and `loading` attributes have nothing to do with chunk loading.
questions.asked: Preloading on intent is a cheap UX win; mentioning it shows practical performance experience.

questions.q: Which split usually gives the biggest first-load win in a single-page React app?
choices: Splitting each small component into its own chunk
Splitting by route, so each page loads its own code
Splitting React itself into a separate vendor chunk
Splitting CSS files per component with dynamic imports
questions.why: Users visit one route at a time, so route-level chunks keep most code off the first load with few boundaries to manage. Splitting tiny components creates request overhead and loading flashes. A vendor chunk helps caching but does not cut what the first page needs.
questions.asked: The expected default answer for "how would you reduce the initial bundle?".

questions.q: A search box triggers an API call per keystroke and filters a large rendered list. What do debouncing and `useDeferredValue` each fix?
choices: Each cuts network requests; deferring also cancels in-flight ones
Debouncing keeps typing smooth; deferring reduces the request count
Debouncing cuts requests; deferring keeps typing responsive
Neither cuts requests; that needs an `AbortController` per keystroke
questions.why: Debouncing waits for a pause, so fewer requests fire. `useDeferredValue` makes React render the expensive list at lower priority so the input stays responsive, but it still renders every value eventually and sends nothing less over the network. They solve different problems and are often combined.
questions.asked: Separates people who reach for transitions for everything from those who know what each tool addresses.

questions.q: Why is `key={Math.random()}` on list items a performance problem?
choices: Random keys collide, so React renders some rows twice
Every render gives every row a new key, so all rows remount
React has to sort the keys, which is slow for random numbers
Keys must be strings, so React converts each number on render
questions.why: A changed key means "a different item", so React destroys and recreates every row on each render: DOM rebuilt, state lost, focus lost. Keys need to be stable identifiers from the data.
questions.asked: Easy points, but a surprising number of candidates think any unique key is fine.

questions.q: A component filters and sorts 10,000 rows on each render, and it re-renders often for unrelated reasons. Which fix fits best?
questions.code: const visible = rows.filter(matches(query)).sort(byDate);
choices: Move the filter into an effect that writes the result to state
Store the sorted rows in a ref so they are computed only once
Wrap the component in `memo` so the filter never runs again
Wrap it in `useMemo` keyed on `rows` and `query`
questions.why: `useMemo` recomputes only when its inputs change, which is exactly what an expensive derived value needs. An effect adds an extra render and a stale frame; a ref would go stale when `rows` changes; `memo` still re-runs everything when props change.
questions.asked: The textbook case for `useMemo`; interviewers want "derived, expensive, frequently re-rendered".

questions.q: Why does wrapping this JSX in `useMemo` stop `Chart` re-rendering when `App` re-renders for other reasons?
questions.code:
const chart = useMemo(() => <Chart data={data} />, [data]);
return <>{chart}<Filters /></>;
choices: React skips a child given the very same element object
The memoised element is rendered on a separate, lower-priority lane
`useMemo` also caches the rendered DOM output, not only the element
Elements from `useMemo` are treated as `memo` components with deep equality
questions.why: When a parent re-renders and a child element is referentially identical to the previous one, React bails out of rendering that subtree. That is the same reason `children` passed from above do not re-render. It is shallow identity, not deep comparison or DOM caching.
questions.asked: An advanced detail that shows you know the real bail-out rule behind `memo` and composition.

questions.q: A page freezes for 2 seconds while parsing a large CSV the user uploads. Which fix keeps the UI responsive?
choices: Wrap the parse call in `startTransition` so React can interrupt it
Run the parse in a Web Worker and post the result back
Move the parse into `useEffect` so it runs after paint
Wrap the parsing component in `memo` so it renders once
questions.why: Transitions only make React's own rendering interruptible; a synchronous 2 s function still blocks the main thread. Running it after paint in an effect still freezes the page. Only moving the work off the main thread (a worker) or chunking it keeps input responsive.
questions.asked: Checks you know the limits of React's scheduling: it cannot interrupt your own long-running code.

questions.q: What does "Highlight updates when components render" in React DevTools show you?
choices: Components whose DOM output changed since the last commit
Components that rendered, even if the DOM stayed the same
Components with effects that ran during the last commit
Components whose props failed their TypeScript types
questions.why: It flashes an outline around every component that rendered, which makes wasted renders visible even when the DOM stays the same. It is a quick way to spot state held too high before opening the Profiler.
questions.asked: A practical debugging tool that shows you can find render problems without guessing.

questions.q: Why does `memo` do nothing for `Row` here?
choices: `memo` is ignored for components rendered inside `map`
`key` changes every render, so the memo cache is cleared
`style` and `onSelect` are new objects each render
`row` objects are compared deeply and always differ
questions.why: The inline object and arrow function are new references on each render, so the shallow prop comparison always fails. Hoist the style to a constant and pass a stable `onSelect(id)` callback (or rely on the React Compiler). `key` is stable here, and `memo` is shallow.
questions.asked: The most common reason memoisation "doesn't work"; interviewers expect you to spot it instantly.

questions.q: A large form with 80 controlled inputs lags on every keystroke. Which change targets the cause?
choices: Replace `useState` with `useReducer` in the form component
Wrap the whole form in `Suspense` so typing is deferred
Debounce every `onChange` so state updates less often
Keep each field's state local, or use uncontrolled inputs
questions.why: One big state object at the form root means every keystroke re-renders all 80 fields. Localising state per field, or letting the DOM hold values (as React Hook Form does), limits each keystroke to one field. `useReducer` changes the API, not the render scope; debouncing input makes typing feel broken.
questions.asked: Links form architecture to render cost, which is why form libraries exist.

questions.q: A chat window renders 5,000 messages and scrolling stutters. Which approach fits best?
choices: Virtualise it so only nearby messages are mounted
Wrap each message in `memo` so scrolling skips their renders
Add `will-change: transform` to every message element
Render the messages inside a portal to isolate their layout
questions.why: Scrolling does not re-render React components, so `memo` cannot help: the cost is thousands of DOM nodes for layout and paint. Virtualisation cuts the node count. Applying `will-change` to thousands of nodes adds memory and can make it worse.
questions.asked: Distinguishes render cost from DOM size cost, which many candidates conflate.

questions.q: Why should a scroll or resize handler that updates state be throttled with `requestAnimationFrame`?
choices: React ignores state updates that arrive faster than once per frame
Browsers stop firing scroll events if handlers take longer than 16 ms
They fire many times per frame, but only one frame paints
State updates from native listeners are not batched in React 19
questions.why: Scroll and resize can fire far more often than the screen repaints, so updating state on each event wastes renders nobody sees. Scheduling one update per animation frame matches the display rate. React 18+ batches all updates, and it does not drop fast ones.
questions.asked: Shows you connect React rendering with the browser's frame budget.

questions.q: You memoise every component in the app "just in case". What is the main cost?
choices: Memoised components cannot use context or read refs
Extra code and comparisons, often for no measurable gain
React disables concurrent rendering for memoised trees
Memoised components always render twice in production
questions.why: Each `memo` adds a prop comparison and each `useMemo` adds dependency bookkeeping and bugs when deps are wrong; if props change anyway, it is all overhead. Measure, fix state placement, then memoise hot spots, or let the React Compiler do it.
questions.asked: Interviewers probe for judgement: memoisation is a tool with costs, not a default.

questions.q: A route renders a heavy `ReportView` behind a tab that most users never open. What does rendering it conditionally achieve over hiding it with CSS?
choices: Hiding with CSS unmounts it too, so the two are identical
The conditional version keeps its state when you switch tabs away
The CSS version is faster, because hidden elements skip rendering
The report is never rendered or fetched until the tab is chosen
questions.why: With the `&&` version, `ReportView` does not exist until selected, so its render and effects never run. The `hidden` version mounts it immediately (running its effects and fetches) but preserves its state across tab switches. React 19.2's `<Activity mode="hidden">` gives preserved state while deferring the work.
questions.asked: A trade-off question: mount cost versus preserved state. Mentioning `<Activity>` shows current knowledge.

questions.q: In React 19.2, what does wrapping a panel in `<Activity mode="hidden">` do?
choices: Unmounts the panel but keeps its DOM in a cache for later
Keeps the panel mounted and visible but pauses its re-renders
Hides it, keeps its state, and unmounts its effects
Renders the panel on the server and streams it in when shown
questions.why: `<Activity>` hides its children, preserves their state and DOM, and unmounts their effects while hidden; updates are rendered at low priority. It gives you "hidden tab keeps its form input" without the running effects that CSS hiding would leave on.
questions.asked: A 2025 addition; knowing it signals you track React releases.

questions.q: In the browser, what does `Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form))` produce for this form when nothing is changed?
questions.code:
<form>
  <input name="email" defaultValue="a@b.co" />
  <input name="plan" defaultValue="pro" disabled />
  <input type="checkbox" name="terms" />
</form>
choices: `{ email: "a@b.co", plan: "pro", terms: "off" }`
`{ email: "a@b.co", plan: "pro", terms: false }`
`{ email: "a@b.co" }`
`{ email: "a@b.co", terms: null }`
questions.why: Disabled controls and unchecked checkboxes are not submitted, so both keys are simply missing. Use `readOnly` if a value must be sent but not edited, and treat a missing checkbox key as false on the server.
questions.asked: A classic source of "the field is missing on the server" bugs once teams move to FormData and actions.

questions.q: A controlled `<input type="number">` feeds `setQty(e.target.value)`. Later `qty + 1` shows `"21"` for an input of 2. Why?
choices: React converts number inputs to strings to keep them controlled
`e.target.value` is always a string, even for number inputs
Number inputs return the previous value until the input blurs
The `+` operator concatenates whenever state came from an event
questions.why: Input values are strings in the DOM regardless of `type`. Convert explicitly (`Number(v)` or `e.target.valueAsNumber`), and remember an empty field gives `""` or `NaN`, so the state type should allow "empty".
questions.asked: Easy, but it shows you have debugged real forms rather than only demo ones.

questions.q: In a React form, the user presses Enter in the email field. Which handler should contain the save logic so this and clicking Save behave the same?
questions.code:
<form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
  <input name="email" />
  <button type="submit" onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>
</form>
choices: `handleClick`, because Enter triggers a click on the input
`handleSubmit`, which fires for Enter and for the button
An `onKeyDown` on the input that checks for the Enter key
Both, since Enter only fires `onSubmit` and a click only `onClick`
questions.why: Implicit submission means Enter in a text field submits the form, and a submit button click also fires `submit`. Putting logic in `onSubmit` covers both paths plus native validation; a click handler misses keyboard users who press Enter.
questions.asked: Checks you use the form element as intended, which also matters for accessibility.

questions.q: Clicking "Cancel" in this React form unexpectedly saves it. Why?
questions.code:
<form onSubmit={save}>
  <input name="title" />
  <button onClick={close}>Cancel</button>
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>
choices: A `<button>` inside a form defaults to `type="submit"`
React runs `onSubmit` for every click inside a form
`close` returns a value, which React treats as a submit
The first button in a form is always the default action
questions.why: Buttons default to `type="submit"`, so Cancel submits the form after `close` runs. Give non-submit buttons `type="button"`. Enter-key submission uses the first submit button, which is why the default matters.
questions.asked: A classic bug reviewers catch in forms; it shows attention to HTML semantics in React.

questions.q: In React 19, what happens to this uncontrolled input after the form action finishes successfully?
questions.code:
<form action={async (fd) => { await save(fd.get("note")); }}>
  <input name="note" defaultValue="" />
  <button>Add</button>
</form>
choices: It keeps the typed text until the component unmounts
It is reset to its default value automatically
It is cleared before the action runs, so `fd` is empty
It is disabled until the page is reloaded
questions.why: When a function is passed to `<form action>`, React resets the form's uncontrolled fields after the action completes, which suits "add a note" flows. Controlled inputs keep whatever their state says. Use `requestFormReset` for manual control.
questions.asked: A React 19 behaviour change that surprises people migrating from `onSubmit` handlers.

questions.q: Why is client-side validation in a React form not enough on its own?
choices: Browsers skip client-side checks when the page is served over HTTPS
Anyone can call the API directly, so the server must validate too
React discards validation state whenever the component re-renders
Client validation only runs for fields that the user has focused
questions.why: Client validation is for fast feedback; it offers no protection because requests can be sent with curl or a modified page. The server re-validates everything and returns field errors the form can display. Sharing one schema keeps the two consistent.
questions.asked: Basic, but a wrong answer here is a security red flag.

questions.q: After a successful upload, the chosen file name still shows in this input. What is the usual React fix?
questions.code: <input type="file" onChange={(e) => setFile(e.target.files[0])} />
choices: Set `value={file?.name ?? ""}` so React controls the input
Change a `key` on the input (or reset the form) to clear it
Call `setFile(null)`, which also clears the browser input
Set `files={[]}` on the input to drop the chosen file
questions.why: Script can clear a file input but never set its value, so React cannot control it and clearing your state does not touch the DOM. Remounting with a new key, calling `form.reset()`, or setting `ref.current.value = ""` clears it; `files` is not a settable prop.
questions.asked: Upload forms are common in CRUD apps; this checks you know the platform limits behind uncontrolled file inputs.

questions.q: What format does a controlled `<input type="date">` give you in `e.target.value`, regardless of the user's locale?
choices: The date as displayed, such as `24/09/2026` in the UK
A `Date` object at local midnight on the chosen day
A timestamp in milliseconds since the Unix epoch
A string in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, such as `2026-09-24`
questions.why: The display follows the locale but the value is always an ISO date string, or `""` when empty. Parsing it with `new Date("2026-09-24")` gives UTC midnight, which can shift the day in some time zones, so keep it as a string until you need a `Date`.
questions.asked: Date handling bugs are common in CRUD forms; this probes whether you have met them.

questions.q: A form has Country and Region selects, and the region list depends on the country. What should happen when the country changes?
choices: Keep the region, since the server will reject an invalid pair anyway
Reset the region, since the old one may not exist in the new list
Disable the country select until the region is chosen again
Reload the page so both selects start from default values
questions.why: Dependent fields must be cleared (or revalidated) when their parent changes, otherwise the form holds an impossible combination the user cannot see. Do it in the country change handler, not in an effect, so both updates happen in one render.
questions.asked: Tests practical form design and whether you reach for handlers rather than effects.

questions.q: A sign-up form checks "username available?" as the user types. Which design is sound?
choices: Check on every keystroke and show the latest response that comes back
Check only on submit, because async validation confuses users
Debounce, drop stale replies, show pending, re-check on submit
Check once on blur, then cache that answer for the rest of the session
questions.why: Debouncing limits requests, cancelling or ignoring stale responses prevents an old "available" overwriting a newer "taken", and a pending state explains the delay. The server must still enforce uniqueness at submit because the name can be taken in between.
questions.asked: Combines race conditions, UX and server authority in one small feature, which is why it is popular.

questions.q: A five-step checkout wizard keeps each step in its own component. Where should the collected answers live?
choices: In each step's own state, read back through refs on the last step
In `localStorage`, written by each step and read on submit
In a parent or reducer that owns the answers and current step
In URL search params, one param per field across all the steps
questions.why: Steps unmount as the user moves on, so their local state is lost; the parent that outlives them must own the data. A reducer keeps transitions (next, back, edit step 2) explicit. The URL suits the step number, not every field, and storage is for drafts that must survive reloads.
questions.asked: A system-design-in-miniature question that shows how you reason about component lifetimes.

questions.q: An edit form should warn users with unsaved changes before they leave. Which pair of mechanisms covers both cases?
choices: `beforeunload` for tab closes plus a router blocker for links
A `window.confirm` in `useEffect` cleanup, which runs on any navigation
An `onBlur` on the form that saves the draft to local storage
A `visibilitychange` listener that cancels navigation when hidden
questions.why: Closing or reloading the tab only fires `beforeunload` (with the browser's generic prompt); client-side route changes never fire it, so the router's blocking API (`useBlocker` in React Router) handles those. Effect cleanup cannot cancel anything, it just runs after the fact.
questions.asked: A real product requirement; knowing both halves shows you have implemented it.

questions.q: What does "dirty" mean for a form field, and why track it?
choices: The field failed validation, so it is shown with an error style
The field has been focused, so errors may now be shown for it
The field is waiting on async validation from the server
It differs from its initial value; drives Save and leave warnings
questions.why: Dirty means changed from the default. It powers "disable Save until something changed", "send only changed fields in a PATCH", and unsaved-changes warnings. Focused-then-left is "touched", a separate flag used for error timing.
questions.asked: Form libraries expose dirty and touched separately; knowing both shows you have used them.

questions.q: An edit form sends `PATCH /users/7`. Why send only the dirty fields rather than the whole form?
choices: PATCH requests are limited to a few hundred bytes by most servers
It avoids overwriting fields someone else changed meanwhile
Sending unchanged fields makes the server run validation twice
Browsers cache PATCH bodies, so unchanged fields would be ignored
questions.why: Sending stale copies of untouched fields can silently revert someone else's edits (lost update). Sending only changes shrinks that window; an ETag or version check closes it fully. Size limits and caching have nothing to do with it.
questions.asked: Links a front-end choice to a data integrity problem, which interviewers value.

questions.q: A form library's `reset(user)` is called when fresh `user` data arrives. What problem does that solve?
choices: It sets new defaults, so dirty checks compare with saved data
It clears validation errors caused by typing too quickly
It forces every input to become controlled by React state
It sends the form data to the server once more to confirm it
questions.why: Default values are read once at mount; if data loads later, `reset` updates both field values and the baseline used for dirty checks. Calling it after a successful save also makes the form clean again.
questions.asked: The async-default-values problem is one of the most common form-library questions on the job.
