questions.q: Which is the better place to trim whitespace and convert "12.50" to a number in a form?
choices: In each input's `onChange`, so state always holds the final value
In a `useEffect` that normalises state after each render
At submit or in the validation schema, as a parse step
On the server only, since the client should send raw input
questions.why: Normalising on every keystroke fights the user (you cannot type a trailing space or "12."). Parsing at the boundary, often with a schema that trims and coerces, keeps the input free and the output clean; the server still validates what arrives.
questions.asked: Shows you think about the difference between what users type and what the app stores.

questions.q: Why is a single form-level error message ("Something is wrong") worse than field-level errors for a long form?
choices: Screen readers cannot read errors that are not attached to fields
Browsers block form submission while a form-level message is shown
Users have to hunt for the field; field errors say what and where
React cannot re-render a form-level error without remounting it
questions.why: Good errors name the field and the fix ("Postcode must be 5 digits") next to the input, linked with `aria-describedby`. A summary at the top helps for long forms, but only when it links to those specific fields.
questions.asked: Error UX is part of every CRUD job; interviewers want concrete, actionable messages.

questions.q: Why must an error boundary be a class component (or come from a library such as `react-error-boundary`)?
choices: Function components cannot render `children` returned from a catch
There is no hook equivalent of `getDerivedStateFromError` yet
Class components render faster, which matters during an error
Errors propagate only through class components in the tree
questions.why: Catching render errors relies on the class lifecycle methods `static getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch`; React 19 still has no hook for them. Most teams use `react-error-boundary`, which wraps that class with a friendlier API.
questions.asked: Easy confirmation you have actually written or used an error boundary.

questions.q: In an error boundary class, what are `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch` each for?
choices: The first logs the error; the second switches to the fallback UI
The first handles render errors; the second handles effect errors
The first runs on the server; the second runs only in the browser
The first sets fallback state; the second reports the error
questions.why: `getDerivedStateFromError` is a pure static method that returns state for the fallback render; `componentDidCatch` runs after commit with the error and component stack, so it is where side effects such as logging go. Both handle the same errors.
questions.asked: Separating the pure part from the side-effect part mirrors how React is designed, which is what the question checks.

questions.q: In React 19 with `createRoot`, a render error is thrown and no error boundary catches it. What does the user see?
choices: The whole app unmounts, leaving an empty root element
Only the component that threw is removed from the screen
The last successfully rendered UI stays, frozen in place
React retries the render up to three times, then shows nothing
questions.why: Since React 16, an uncaught render error unmounts the whole tree, because showing a half-broken UI can be worse than showing nothing. That is why every app needs at least a root-level boundary with a useful fallback.
questions.asked: Explains why error boundaries are not optional, which is usually the point of the question.

questions.q: Where should error boundaries go in a typical dashboard app?
choices: Only one at the root, so every error shows the same fallback page
Around every component, so no error can ever escape its source
At the root, around each route, and around independent widgets
Only around components that fetch data, since only they can fail
questions.why: A root boundary is the safety net, route boundaries keep navigation working when one page breaks, and widget boundaries let a failing chart show "Couldn't load" while the rest works. Wrapping every component adds noise, and render bugs are not limited to fetching components.
questions.asked: Boundary granularity is a design question; interviewers want reasoning about blast radius.

questions.q: An async click handler fails. How can you show it in the nearest error boundary's fallback?
choices: Rethrow `err` inside the catch; the boundary catches async errors
Call `console.error(err)`, which React routes to the nearest boundary
Call `setState(() => { throw err; })` to throw it in render
Call `window.onerror(err)`, which React forwards to the boundary
questions.why: Boundaries only catch errors thrown while rendering. Throwing from a state updater (or `showBoundary` in `react-error-boundary`) moves the error into the next render. Rethrowing from an async handler just produces an unhandled rejection, and logging is only logging. (React 19 also routes errors thrown inside a transition action to boundaries.)
questions.asked: A deeper probe that shows you know exactly which errors boundaries see and how to route others to them.

questions.q: In React 19, what are the `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError` options of `createRoot` for?
choices: Replacing error boundaries with a single root-level fallback UI
Retrying failed renders before an error boundary is shown
Reporting errors, such as sending them to a logging service
Catching errors from event handlers and async code as well
questions.why: They are central hooks for reporting: `onCaughtError` fires for errors a boundary handled and `onUncaughtError` for those that reached the root. They do not render UI or catch handler errors; boundaries still decide what the user sees.
questions.asked: Shows awareness of React 19's error reporting hooks and how monitoring fits in.

questions.q: After a deploy, users who kept a tab open get a blank page when they open a lazily loaded route. What is happening, and what is a good fix?
choices: The old chunk is gone; catch it in a boundary offering reload
The browser cached the new chunk; clear local storage on each deploy
React refuses to load chunks built by another version; pin React
The service worker is blocking it; turn off `Suspense` for routes
questions.why: Hashed chunk names change on each deploy, so an old page's `import()` can 404 and reject. A route error boundary that recognises the chunk-load failure and offers (or does) a reload recovers cleanly; keeping old assets for a while also helps.
questions.asked: A real production issue in every code-split SPA; knowing it signals shipping experience.

questions.q: A background refetch of the orders list fails, but the list loaded fine a minute ago. What is the best UX?
choices: Replace the list with a full-page error until the next fetch succeeds
Keep the stale list and show a small "Couldn't refresh, retry" notice
Hide the failure, since the user already has data on screen
Clear the list and show the empty state so nothing wrong is shown
questions.why: Stale data is still useful; replacing it with an error punishes the user for a transient failure, and hiding it means they may act on old data unknowingly. Query libraries keep `data` and `error` side by side precisely so you can show both.
questions.asked: Good error UX is a mid-level expectation; this checks you distinguish initial-load and refresh failures.

questions.q: Which error message is best to show when saving a customer fails with a 409 Conflict?
choices: "Error 409: Conflict. The request could not be completed."
"Something went wrong. Please try again later."
"Request failed: PUT /customers/42 returned 409"
"Someone else changed this customer. Reload to see their changes."
questions.why: A useful message says what happened in the user's terms and what they can do next. Status codes and URLs mean nothing to most users (log them instead), and a generic "try again" is wrong here because retrying the same stale write will conflict again.
questions.asked: Checks that you translate technical failures into actionable UI.

questions.q: A list screen can end in "no results" or in "request failed". Why render them as different states?
choices: React cannot render an empty array, so errors must be rendered instead
They need different actions: clear filters versus retry or report
Error states must be rendered by an error boundary, not the list
Empty states are only needed when the list uses pagination
questions.why: Showing "No orders" when the request failed tells the user something false, and they may act on it. An empty state suggests next steps (clear filters, create one); an error state explains the failure and offers retry. They come from different data (`data.length === 0` vs `error`).
questions.asked: A simple state-modelling question that reveals whether you treat failure as a first-class state.

questions.q: When should an error toast not auto-dismiss after a few seconds?
choices: When the user must act on it, such as a failed payment
When the page also shows a loading spinner at the same time
When the error came from a GET rather than a POST request
When the toast is announced by a screen reader live region
questions.why: Auto-dismissing hides errors the user may not have read, and WCAG 2.2.1 requires users can extend or disable time limits. Transient confirmations can fade; errors that need action should stay (or be shown inline) until dismissed.
questions.asked: Links UX judgement with accessibility requirements, which interviewers like to see together.

questions.q: A reusable `TextField` component hard-codes `<label htmlFor="email">` and `<input id="email">`. What breaks when a page renders two of them?
choices: React throws because two sibling elements share one `key`
The ids clash, so the second label targets the first input
The second input is rendered uncontrolled and ignores `value`
Screen readers skip both labels because the id is not unique
questions.why: DOM ids must be unique; with duplicates, `htmlFor` and `aria-describedby` resolve to the first match, so clicking or announcing the second label targets the wrong input. Generate ids with `useId()` so each instance gets its own; React does not warn about duplicate DOM ids at all.
questions.asked: Shows you think about components as reusable units rather than one-off markup.

questions.q: A user deletes a row by pressing its Delete button with the keyboard. The row, and the focused button, disappear. What should the component do next?
choices: Nothing, because the browser moves focus to the next row itself
Call `window.scrollTo(0, 0)` so the user starts again from the top
Move focus on purpose, to the next row or the list heading
Blur the active element so no stale focus ring is left on screen
questions.why: When the focused element is removed, focus falls back to `<body>`, so keyboard and screen-reader users lose their place and must tab from the top. Moving focus to a sensible neighbour keeps them where they were; the browser does not do this for you.
questions.asked: Focus management after destructive actions is where accessible CRUD screens are won or lost.

questions.q: A "Saved" message is rendered like this after a successful save, but screen readers never announce it. Why?
choices: The region appears already filled, so there is no change to announce
`role="status"` only works on `<output>` elements, not on a `<div>`
Live regions are only announced when the element also has keyboard focus
Screen readers ignore live-region text that is shorter than a full sentence
questions.why: Assistive technology announces changes to an existing live region. Render the empty `role="status"` (or `aria-live="polite"`) container up front and change only its text; a region that appears already filled is often missed.
questions.asked: Toasts and inline "saved" feedback are everywhere, and most implementations are silent to screen readers.

questions.q:
Which problem does `
Options
` have that `` does not?
choices: The `div` fires `onClick` twice on touch devices
The `div` cannot be focused or activated with Enter or Space
React does not attach click listeners to non-interactive DOM elements
The `div` blocks the click from bubbling to parent handlers
questions.why: A `div` has no role, is not in the tab order and ignores Enter and Space, so keyboard and screen-reader users cannot use it. Making it work needs `role`, `tabIndex` and key handlers, which a native button gives you free; React happily attaches the click handler either way.
questions.asked: The most common accessibility bug in React code reviews; interviewers want the native-element instinct.

questions.q: In a client-side routed React app, a screen-reader user follows a link to another page and hears nothing. What is the usual fix?
choices: Force a full page reload on each navigation so the reader restarts
Add `aria-live="assertive"` to the whole `<main>` element
Set `tabIndex={-1}` on every link so focus stays predictable
Update `document.title` and focus the new page heading
questions.why: A full load makes the reader announce the new page; a client-side route swap does not. Updating the title and focusing the page heading (with `tabIndex={-1}`) restores that cue; an assertive live region on `main` would read the whole page out on every change.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what an SPA takes away compared with plain page loads.

questions.q: In React 19, why expose a small API with `useImperativeHandle` instead of passing the raw `<input>` node through `ref`?
choices: It is required in React 19, because `ref` can no longer point at DOM nodes
It makes the handle reactive, so parents re-render when `value` changes
Parents get only the actions you support, so internals can change safely
It lets the parent read `value` synchronously without a re-render
questions.why: An imperative handle is a deliberate, narrow API: parents can call `focus` and `clear` but cannot style or mutate the node, so you can restructure the component later. Refs still point at DOM nodes fine in React 19, and a handle is not reactive.
questions.asked: Separates people who know refs are an escape hatch from those who reach for them by default.

questions.q: In React 19, what is logged when this `Panel` unmounts?
questions.code:
<div ref={(node) => {
  console.log("attach", node !== null);
  return () => console.log("cleanup");
}} />
choices: "cleanup" only, since the cleanup replaces the null call
"attach false" and then "cleanup"
"attach false" only, because cleanup functions are ignored on refs
Nothing, because callback refs are not called on unmount
questions.why: React 19 lets a callback ref return a cleanup function; when it does, React calls the cleanup on detach instead of calling the ref with `null`. Code written for older versions that expects a `null` call will not see one once it returns a cleanup.
questions.asked: Checks you have kept up with React 19 and can set up observers on a node without leaks.

questions.q: A component tracks `isLoading`, `isError` and `isSuccess` as three separate booleans. What is the main problem with this shape?
choices: Three `useState` calls make the component render three times per update
It allows impossible combinations, such as loading and error at once
Booleans cannot be passed through context without being memoised
React batches only the first state update, so the others are lost
questions.why: Independent flags can drift into states the UI cannot represent, and each transition must remember to reset the others. A single `status: "idle" | "loading" | "error" | "success"` makes illegal states unrepresentable; React batches all the updates, so render count is not the issue.
questions.asked: A modelling question in disguise: strong answers mention discriminated unions or a reducer.

questions.q: When is `useReducer` a better fit than several `useState` calls?
choices: Whenever a component has more than three pieces of state
When named events change several related fields together
When the state must survive the component unmounting and remounting
When the state is shared by sibling components without lifting it up
questions.why: A reducer centralises transitions such as "submitted" or "itemRemoved" that touch several fields at once, and it can be unit-tested as a pure function. It gives no persistence or sharing on its own; count of fields is a poor rule of thumb.
questions.asked: Interviewers want a reason, not "for complex state", so name transitions and testability.

questions.q: A list shows optimistic toggles. The user toggles item 5 twice quickly; the first request fails and the handler restores the snapshot it took before that request. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing, because each handler restores only its own snapshot
The rollback wipes out the second toggle, so the UI drifts
React discards the second click because a state update is already pending
The second request is cancelled by the browser when the first one fails
questions.why: A whole-value snapshot taken before request 1 predates toggle 2, so restoring it silently undoes a change that may have succeeded. Roll back only the failed change, or refetch the item when mutations settle; React does not drop the second click.
questions.asked: Optimistic UI is easy to demo and hard to get right under concurrency; this is the follow-up that separates levels.

questions.q: A custom hook `useToggle` returns `[on, toggle]` rather than `{ on, toggle }`. What does the tuple give callers?
choices: Faster renders, because arrays are cheaper to compare than objects
Automatic memoisation of `toggle` across renders
Freedom to name both values at each call site, as with `useState`
Type inference, which TypeScript cannot provide for returned object literals
questions.why: Array destructuring lets each call site pick names like `[menuOpen, toggleMenu]` without aliasing. Objects read better once a hook returns more than two or three things; neither form memoises anything by itself.
questions.asked: A light API-design question; mentioning when to switch to an object shows judgement.

questions.q: In React 19, why does this component crash with "Maximum update depth exceeded"?
choices: `store.subscribe` must be wrapped in `useCallback` before it is passed
`useSyncExternalStore` cannot return objects, only primitive values
The store has to call its listeners once during subscribe
`getSnapshot` returns a new object each call, so it never looks stable
questions.why: React compares snapshots with `Object.is`; a fresh object every call looks like a change every time, so it re-renders forever (React also warns that the result should be cached). Return a stored, immutable snapshot, or a primitive like `store.count`. A stable `subscribe` avoids resubscribing but does not fix this.
questions.asked: Anyone who has written a small store adapter has hit this; it tests understanding of snapshot identity.

questions.q: A search box writes `?q=` to the URL on every keystroke with a push navigation. What is the user-visible problem, and the fix?
choices: Back steps through every keystroke; replace the entry instead
The page reloads on each keystroke; debounce the input by 300 ms
The query is lost on refresh; move it to `sessionStorage`
The URL grows without limit; store only the first ten characters
questions.why: Each push adds a history entry, so Back walks through "a", "ad", "ada". Replacing the current entry (for example `setSearchParams(p, { replace: true })`) keeps the URL shareable without polluting history; a client-side router does not reload the page.
questions.asked: URL-as-state is a senior-leaning habit; knowing push versus replace shows you have shipped it.

questions.q: New to-do items are created on the client and have no server id yet. What should they use as their list `key`?
choices: The array index, since new items are always appended
The item text, because users rarely add the same to-do twice
An id made once at creation, e.g. `crypto.randomUUID()`
`Date.now()` computed inside the `map` while rendering
questions.why: A key must be stable and unique for the item's lifetime, so generate it once when the item is created and store it with the item. Indexes break on delete or reorder, text can repeat, and anything computed during render changes every render.
questions.asked: Checks you understand keys as identity, not as a warning to silence.

questions.q: An optimistic "add comment" renders the new row with `key={comment.id}`, where the temporary id is swapped for the server id on success. The row's edit box loses focus at that moment. Why?
choices: Replacing the array triggers a full list remount regardless of keys
Focus is lost because the server response arrives outside an event handler
React blurs inputs whenever a parent receives new props during a transition
The key changes, so React unmounts the old row and mounts a new one
questions.why: A new key is a new identity to React, so the row and its DOM, focus and local state are thrown away. Keep a stable client id as the key for the row's whole life and store the server id as a separate field; React reuses rows whose keys stay the same.
questions.asked: A real optimistic-UI bug that only people who have built one tend to recognise.

questions.q: The Submit button stays `disabled` until every field in a long form is valid. What is the main problem with that pattern?
choices: Disabled buttons are still submitted, so the check is bypassed anyway
Users get no reason why, and keyboard users may not find it
React cannot re-enable a button once it has rendered as disabled
Browsers skip native validation on forms that contain a disabled button
questions.why: A greyed-out button gives no reason, and disabled buttons are skipped by Tab, so keyboard users may not find it at all. Keep it enabled, validate on submit, and move focus to the first invalid field with a message. A disabled submit button does block submission; the problem is feedback.
questions.asked: Tests whether you design forms for people who get things wrong, which is everyone.

questions.q: How should a field's error text be connected to its input so screen readers announce it?
questions.code: {error}
choices: `aria-label={error}` replacing the label while the error is shown
`title={error}` so it appears on hover and to assistive technology
`aria-describedby={`${id}-err`}` pointing at the error element
`role="alert"` on the input itself so it is read on every keystroke
questions.why: `aria-describedby` adds the error as the input's description, read after its name when focused, and `aria-invalid` marks the state. Replacing the label with `aria-label` loses the field name, and `title` is unreliable for assistive technology and invisible on touch.
questions.asked: A concrete ARIA question that is easy to verify and common on form-heavy CRUD work.

questions.q: A modal is built on the native `<dialog>` element and opened with `showModal()`. What does the browser give you without extra code?
choices: Closing when the user clicks the backdrop, plus body scroll locking
An accessible name taken from the first heading inside the dialog
Top-layer rendering, an inert page behind it and Escape to close
A portal into `document.body`, so parent styles no longer apply
questions.why: `showModal()` puts the dialog in the top layer (no z-index fights), makes the rest of the page inert and closes on Escape via the `cancel` event. Backdrop clicks and scroll locking still need code, and you still name the dialog with `aria-labelledby`.
questions.asked: Knowing what the platform now does for modals saves a dependency and a class of focus bugs.

questions.q: In React 19, a user profile renders `<a href={user.website}>`. An attacker sets their website to `javascript:stealCookies()`. What happens when a visitor clicks it?
choices: The script runs, because React passes attribute strings through untouched
React refuses to render the `<a>` element and logs a warning instead
The browser blocks it, because inline `javascript:` URLs are always disabled
Nothing runs, because React replaces the URL with one that throws an error
questions.why: React 19 rewrites `javascript:` URLs in attributes like `href` to a URL that throws "React has blocked a javascript: URL", while still rendering the link. Browsers do run such URLs without a strict CSP, so you should still validate URLs to `http:`/`https:` on input.
questions.asked: A security follow-up to `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` that shows you know where React does and does not protect you.

questions.q: An icon-only button renders `<button onClick={close}><XIcon /></button>`. What does it need for screen-reader users?
choices: An accessible name, such as `aria-label="Close"`
A `role="button"` attribute, since the button has no text
A `tabIndex={0}`, so that the icon can receive focus
An `alt` attribute on the `<button>` describing the icon
questions.why: Without text, the button is announced as just "button". An `aria-label` (or visually hidden text) gives it a name; native buttons already have the role and are focusable, and `alt` belongs on images, not buttons.
questions.asked: The quickest accessibility check an interviewer can make on your component code.

questions.q: A toolbar has eight buttons. Why do accessible toolbars use a "roving tabindex" instead of leaving every button in the tab order?
choices: Browsers cap the tab order at a few focusable elements per landmark
One Tab stop enters the toolbar and arrow keys move within it
It stops screen readers announcing the buttons more than once
React re-renders fewer buttons when only one has `tabIndex={0}`
questions.why: Only the active item has `tabIndex={0}` and the rest have `-1`, so Tab moves past the whole widget in one step and arrows move between items, as in native composite controls. It is about keyboard efficiency, not render cost or announcement.
questions.asked: Composite widgets (tabs, toolbars, grids) come up whenever you build design-system components.

questions.q: A settings page opens an "Edit address" modal. Why might you store `?edit=address` in the URL instead of in local `useState`?
choices: Modals rendered from the URL skip the portal and render faster
React Router closes the modal automatically on unmount
Local state inside a modal is always reset when the modal closes
The modal can be deep-linked, and Back closes it as users expect
questions.why: URL state survives refresh, can be shared or linked from an email, and makes the browser Back button close the modal instead of leaving the page. It costs a little plumbing, so it suits significant views, not every tooltip.
questions.asked: Shows you consider navigation and shareability as part of UI state design.

questions.q: Components call `fetch("/api/orders")` directly in a dozen places. What does moving those calls into an `api/orders.ts` module mainly buy you?
choices: One place for URLs, headers, errors and types, easy to mock
Automatic request caching, because modules are singletons in the bundle
Smaller bundles, because tree shaking removes duplicate `fetch` calls
Parallel requests, since functions in one module share a connection
questions.why: A thin API layer centralises base URLs, auth headers, error mapping and response types, so a backend change is one edit and tests can mock one module. Being a module does not cache anything, and connection reuse is the browser's job either way.
questions.asked: A small structural choice that shows you have maintained a codebase, not just started one.

questions.q: In React 19.2, a chat effect connects to `roomId` and shows a notification using the current `theme`. Why wrap the notification code in `useEffectEvent`?
choices: It runs the toast after paint instead of during the commit phase
It reads the latest `theme` without making a theme change reconnect
It lets you call `onConnected` during render to avoid an extra state
It memoises `connect`, so StrictMode no longer connects twice in dev
questions.why: An effect event always sees the latest props and state but is not a dependency, so the effect re-runs only when `roomId` changes. Putting `theme` in the dependency array would reconnect on every theme toggle; effect events must not be called during render.
questions.asked: Dependency-array fights are a daily React pain; knowing the 19.2 answer shows you are current.

questions.q: A React app animates list items sliding in. How should it respect users who have asked their OS for less motion?
choices: Honour the `prefers-reduced-motion` media query
Detect screen readers and skip animations only for those users
Keep animations under one second, which the OS setting allows anyway
Add `aria-hidden="true"` to animated elements so they are ignored
questions.why: The `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query (in CSS, or `matchMedia` in JS) reflects the OS setting, and WCAG asks you to avoid non-essential motion for those users. Screen-reader detection is not possible or relevant, and hiding elements from assistive technology is harmful.
questions.asked: An easy accessibility win that interviewers use to see if you know the user preference media queries.

questions.q: An order total is displayed with `"$" + total.toFixed(2)`. The app now ships in Germany and the UK. What is the better approach?
choices: Keep `toFixed(2)` and swap the symbol with a lookup table per country
Store the price as a formatted string in the database for each locale
Use `Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency })`
Round with `Math.round(total * 100) / 100` and append the currency code
questions.why: `Intl.NumberFormat` handles symbol position, decimal and grouping separators ("1.234,50 €" versus "£1,234.50") for any locale and currency. A symbol table misses separators and placement, and storing formatted strings breaks arithmetic.
questions.asked: Money display is on nearly every CRUD screen; this checks you use the platform rather than string hacks.

questions.q: `AuthProvider` calls `useApiClient()`, which reads `ApiContext`. In which order must the providers be nested?
choices: `AuthProvider` outside `ApiProvider`, so auth is available to the client
`ApiProvider` outside, since consumers must sit inside their provider
Either order, because React resolves all contexts before the first render
Side by side as siblings, since nesting providers causes extra renders
questions.why: A component reads the nearest provider above it in the tree, so anything that consumes `ApiContext` (including another provider) must sit inside `ApiProvider`. Outside it, `useApiClient` gets the default value; React does not reorder providers for you.
questions.asked: Provider order bugs are confusing the first time; interviewers check you know how lookup works.

questions.q: In React 19, clicking a tab renders a slow `ReportTab`, and the UI freezes until it is done. How does `startTransition` for the tab change help?
questions.code:
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
const select = (t) => startTransition(() => setTab(t));
choices: It moves the render of `ReportTab` to a Web Worker off the main thread
It caches `ReportTab` so the second visit is instant
The old tab stays responsive while the new one renders
It delays the state update by a frame so the click animation finishes first
questions.why: Transition updates are interruptible: React renders the new tab in the background, keeps showing and responding on the current one, and exposes `isPending` so you can dim it. The render still happens on the main thread and nothing is cached.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the concurrency tools exist for UX, not only for data fetching.

questions.q: A product page wraps its details in `<Suspense>`. Navigating to the next product replaces the visible details with the spinner. What does triggering the navigation in a transition change?
choices: React keeps showing the current product until the next one is ready
The spinner is shown only for requests that take longer than 300 ms
The next product is prefetched when the link is hovered
React retries the suspended request if it fails during the transition
questions.why: Inside a transition, React avoids hiding content that is already revealed behind a fallback; it keeps the old UI on screen (you can show `isPending`) until the new tree can render. There is no built-in threshold, prefetching or retry. Routers do this by wrapping navigations in transitions.
questions.asked: Explains why modern routers feel smooth, and shows you understand Suspense beyond the fallback prop.

questions.q: A custom hook returns `{ start, end }` built fresh on every render. A component uses the result in an effect's dependency array. What happens?
choices: The effect runs once, because React compares objects by their keys
The effect never runs, because objects cannot be dependencies
React warns and falls back to comparing `range` with `JSON.stringify`
It runs after every render, as `range` is a new object each time
questions.why: Dependencies are compared with `Object.is`, so a new object is always "changed" and `load` runs on every render, which can loop if `load` sets state. Depend on the primitive fields, or have the hook memoise what it returns.
questions.asked: The source of many "why is my API called 40 times" bugs; a good answer names referential identity.

questions.q: In React codebases, what is the usual naming convention for a prop that receives a callback versus the function that implements it?
choices: Prop `handleSave`, implementation `onSave`
Prop `onSave`, implementation `handleSave`
Prop `saveCallback`, implementation `saveHandler`
Prop `doSave`, implementation `onSaveClick`
questions.why: Props describe the event the component raises (`onSave`, `onChange`), mirroring DOM events, and the parent implements it as `handleSave`. It is only a convention, but a consistent one makes component APIs predictable and code reviews shorter.
questions.asked: Small, but it shows whether you have worked in a team codebase with conventions.

questions.q: Why does `lazy(() => import("./charts"))` fail when `charts.js` only has `export function Chart()`, and what is the fix?
choices: `lazy` needs the path to end in `.jsx`; rename the file
`lazy` needs a class component; wrap `Chart` in a class
`lazy` needs a default export; map `m.Chart` to `default`
`lazy` needs a static import first; import `Chart` at the top of the file
questions.why: `lazy` expects the promise to resolve to a module whose `default` is a component, so a named export resolves to `undefined` and rendering fails. Mapping the module to `{ default: m.Chart }` keeps the code split; a static import would defeat it.
questions.asked: A practical snag the first time you split a codebase that uses named exports.

questions.q: A notes editor should autosave while the user types. Which design is sound?
choices: Save on every change event so no keystroke can ever be lost
Debounce, send the latest text, flush on unmount or page hide
Save only in a `beforeunload` handler when the user leaves the page
Save every 30 seconds on an interval, whether or not the text has changed
questions.why: Debouncing batches bursts of typing into one request with the newest content, and flushing on unmount or `pagehide` covers leaving mid-pause. Saving per keystroke floods the API, `beforeunload` alone is unreliable on mobile, and blind intervals waste requests.
questions.asked: Autosave comes up in real product work and combines timing, cleanup and API design.

questions.q: An autosave sends `PUT /notes/1` after each pause. Sometimes a slow older request finishes after a newer one and the server keeps the old text. What prevents this?
choices: One save in flight at a time, or a version the server checks
Use `POST` instead of `PUT`, because POST requests are processed in order
Increase the debounce delay so two saves can never be in flight at once
Retry failed saves immediately, which puts the requests back in order
questions.why: Requests can complete out of order, so either serialise saves (one in flight, then send the latest) or include a version or `If-Match` ETag so the server rejects stale writes. A longer debounce narrows the window but cannot close it, and HTTP methods give no ordering guarantee.
questions.asked: A race-condition question grounded in CRUD; strong answers mention optimistic concurrency on the server.

questions.q: A `Dropdown` component's `isOpen` state is read only by the dropdown itself. Where should it live?
choices: In a global store, so any component can close open dropdowns
In the page component, since pages own all interactive state
In a `DropdownContext` at the app root for consistency
Inside `Dropdown` itself, with `useState`
questions.why: Colocating state with the only component that uses it keeps re-renders local and the component self-contained. Lift it only when another component needs to read or change it, for example a parent that closes it on route change.
questions.asked: State placement is the core React design skill, and colocation is the default answer.

questions.q: A table shows page 3 of 40 from a paginated API. Clicking the "Price" header sorts only the 25 visible rows. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing, since sorting what is visible is the expected behaviour
The sort needs `useMemo`, or it is lost on the next render
The API must sort, and the table returns to page 1
The rows need stable keys, or React cannot reorder them
questions.why: Users expect "sort by price" to order the whole dataset, so send the sort to the API (`?sort=price`) and go back to the first page. Sorting one page gives a misleading order; memoising or keys do not change which rows are fetched.
questions.asked: A classic CRUD data-table bug that separates front-end-only thinking from full-stack thinking.

questions.q: An app wraps everything in `<ThemeProvider value="light">`. A sidebar is wrapped in `<ThemeProvider value="dark">`. What theme does a button inside the sidebar read?
choices: "light", because the outermost provider always wins
"dark", because a component reads the nearest provider above it
Whichever provider rendered last during the commit phase
An error, because nesting the same provider twice is not allowed
questions.why: Context lookup walks up from the consumer and stops at the closest matching provider, so nested providers override for their subtree. This is how you theme a section differently or scope a form context per form.
questions.asked: Checks the basic mental model of context before moving on to its performance trade-offs.

questions.q: What is a "Skip to main content" link at the top of a page for?
choices: Letting search engines index the main content before the navigation
Improving load time by deferring the header until after the main content
Letting keyboard users jump past repeated navigation to the content
Giving screen readers a hint to read the page in reverse order
questions.why: A skip link is the first focusable element and jumps focus to `<main>`, so keyboard users do not Tab through dozens of nav links on every page (WCAG "Bypass Blocks"). It has no effect on loading or indexing.
questions.asked: A cheap, standard feature; mentioning it for your app shell signals accessibility awareness.

questions.q: A "Show filters" button toggles a panel below it. Which attribute tells screen-reader users whether the panel is open?
choices: `aria-pressed` on the panel, updated when it opens
`aria-hidden` on the button, mirroring the panel
`aria-expanded` on the button
`aria-selected` on the button, as used for tabs
questions.why: A disclosure button announces its state with `aria-expanded="true|false"`; `aria-controls` points at the panel it toggles. `aria-pressed` is for toggle buttons that are themselves on or off, and `aria-hidden` on the button would remove it from assistive technology.
questions.asked: Disclosure widgets are everywhere; picking the right ARIA state shows you have built them properly.

questions.q: A shipping form has three radio buttons for delivery speed. How should the group get its question text ("Delivery speed") announced?
choices: Put the radios in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`
Give each radio a `title` attribute with the question
Put the question in a `<label>` wrapping all three radios
Add `aria-label` with the question to the form element
questions.why: A `fieldset` with a `legend` names the group, so screen readers announce "Delivery speed" when focus enters it, and each radio keeps its own label. A single label can only label one control, and naming the whole form does not help the group.
questions.asked: Native form semantics are cheaper and more robust than ARIA; interviewers want that instinct.

questions.q: A tooltip measures its own size to decide whether to render above or below its anchor. With `useEffect`, it flickers in the wrong place for a frame. Why does `useLayoutEffect` fix it?
choices: It runs before paint, so the user only sees the final position
It runs on the server as well, so the position is known before hydration
It batches the position update with the parent's render
It gives the measurement a higher priority in the concurrent scheduler
questions.why: `useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after DOM mutation but before paint, so a measure-then-set-state cycle completes before the user sees anything. `useEffect` usually runs after paint, hence the one-frame flash; layout effects do not run on the server at all.
questions.asked: Knowing when the rare `useLayoutEffect` is right shows you understand the render/commit/paint order.

questions.q: Why does `Box` still re-render every time `App` re-renders?
choices: `memo` ignores components whose only prop is `children`
`App` is not memoised, so none of its children can skip rendering
`memo` only skips re-renders when a parent state setter is stable
`hi` is a new element each render, so props differ
questions.why: JSX creates a fresh element object on every render, and `memo` compares props shallowly with `Object.is`, so `children` always looks new. Memoise the element with `useMemo`, or rely on the React Compiler, which caches such JSX for you.
questions.asked: A sharp follow-up for anyone who says "just wrap it in memo"; it tests what memo actually compares.

questions.q: In React 19, a lazily loaded `Chart` sits inside `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>`. Its chunk fails to download. What does the user see?
choices: The spinner forever, because Suspense waits until the chunk arrives
The Suspense fallback swapped for an inline error message
The nearest error boundary's fallback, or a blank root without one
The rest of the page, with `Chart` silently rendered as nothing
questions.why: Suspense only handles the pending state; a rejected load is thrown as an error and travels to the nearest error boundary, so pair every Suspense boundary with one. With no boundary, React 19 unmounts the root and reports it through `onUncaughtError`.
questions.asked: Checks you know loading and failure are separate boundaries, a common gap in lazy-loading answers.

questions.q: An "Add customer" modal is always mounted and toggled with CSS. Reopening it shows the half-typed data from last time. What is the simplest fix?
choices: Clear each field inside a `useEffect` that runs when `open` changes
Store the form data in a global store and reset it on close
Mount the form only while open, or change its `key`
Add `autoComplete="off"` so the browser stops restoring the values
questions.why: Unmounting (or changing `key`) discards the form's state, so every open starts fresh without manual resets. A resetting effect renders stale values first and must be kept in sync with every field; `autoComplete` is unrelated to React state.
questions.asked: Tests whether you reach for React's identity model before writing synchronisation code.

questions.q: You design a reusable `Rating` component. Why call `onChange(4)` rather than passing the raw DOM event up?
choices: DOM events are pooled and cleared, so parents would read `null`
Callers get the value, and your markup stays private
React forbids passing synthetic events to props of other components
Passing events up doubles the number of renders in the parent
questions.why: A value-based `onChange(value)` hides whether the rating is built from radios, buttons or stars, so internals can change without breaking callers. Event pooling was removed in React 17, and passing events is allowed, just leaky.
questions.asked: API design for components is a mid-level signal; this checks you design for the caller.
